<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# Improve the staged experiment

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a snapshot you may repair: inspect its
source, effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward logic,
logs, tracked metrics, and frozen evaluation evidence. Do not assume that an
unusual setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed
behavior.

Use held-out evaluation evidence together with rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training signals. Training reward alone does not establish
held-out health.

## Your job

If you find a defect, fix it in the staged workspace at `/workspace`. **Do not
launch training.** Do not start the experiment, in the foreground or
background, and do not use `nohup`, `&`, `tmux`, `screen`, or any detach
mechanism. The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see below);
anything you launch is wasted and scores nothing. Cheap, non-training checks
are fine.

**Do not use the network.** Do not fetch code, documentation, packages,
or any other material from outside the staged workspace — diagnose and
repair using only what is staged locally.

When you are done, submit a report at `/workspace/report.md`. It must
summarize:

1. **Root cause** — the defect you found, and the evidence in the workspace
   (logs, metrics, code) that connects it to the observed behavior.
2. **Changes** — every file you changed and what you changed in it.
3. **Expected effect** — which metric the fix should move and in which
   direction.

A missing or empty `/workspace/report.md` scores 0.

## What the system will run

After the report is submitted, the system clears `$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs` and runs:

```bash
bash run_training.sh
```

This runs the workspace's `run_training.sh`, which trains with `train.py` and imports the repaired TRL source from `/workspace/src`. The runner files `run_training.sh` and `train.py` are byte-compared against the verifier's pristine copies at grading time; modifying them fails the run. The effective configuration matches `run.py` and `train.sh`:
Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct from `/workspace/model`, 256 GSM8K training questions and 64 held-out questions from `/workspace/data`,
seed 42, 1 GPU process(es), 24 optimizer steps, four completions per prompt, a 256-token completion limit,
gradient accumulation of two microbatches, and four microbatches per generation batch. W&B runs offline.
The wall-clock limit is 1,800 seconds. Model weights, reward logic, data selection and the run budget are fixed by the runner.
Repair the trainer implementation in `src/`.

The verifier requires completed training, at least one nonzero gradient update, and the final held-out evaluation.
It recomputes the accumulation-window objective from this fresh run's recorded per-token probabilities, advantages and completion masks, and requires the logged loss of every optimizer step to agree with the recomputed reference.
This task evaluates optimization correctness and successful execution. Held-out correctness is reported for context and is not a calibrated performance threshold.
Only files from this fresh run are graded. Do not copy, edit or fabricate metrics.
I’ll inspect the staged code and evidence, repair any supported trainer defect, and run only non-training checks. I’ll leave the launch scripts unchanged and write `/workspace/report.md`.

*** Add File: /workspace/report.md
+# Staged experiment review
+
+**Verdict: unhealthy optimization, despite successful execution.** DAPO normalizes each optimizer update by the tokens in an entire generation batch instead of the tokens in that update's actual accumulation window. The frozen held-out result provides context, but does not establish that this defect caused poor correctness or truncation.
+
+## Root cause and evidence
+
+The effective configuration in `train.py` (identical to `run.py`), the launch scripts, and `results/wandb/wandb/offline-run-20261030_173948-wm09yqyi/logs/debug.log` agree: one process, batch size 2, two microbatches per optimizer update, four microbatches per generation batch, four completions per prompt, 256 completion tokens, and `loss_type="dapo"`. The run uses group-normalized binary correctness rewards, beta 0, token importance sampling, no entropy bonus, and no Liger or vLLM backend.
+
+In `src/trl/trainer/grpo_trainer.py`, `_generate_and_score_completions` counts tokens over all eight generated completions. `_prepare_inputs` shuffles and splits this batch into four microbatches, and `split_tensor_dict` copies the same scalar `num_items_in_batch` into every slice. The DAPO loss divides its masked token numerator by that scalar. Only two slices contribute to each optimizer update. Consequently, each update uses tokens from another optimizer window in its denominator. Different completion lengths also make a constant factor of two an inexact repair.
+
+I independently recomputed the clipped surrogate from all 48 frozen files in `results/token_records/`, grouped by optimizer step. For one process, the reference is:
+
+`sum(-min(ratio * advantage, clipped_ratio * advantage) * mask) / sum(mask)`
+
+Both sums cover exactly the two microbatches in that optimizer window. Representative comparisons against `results/metrics_rank0.jsonl` are:
+
+| Optimizer step | Window tokens | Incorrect generation denominator | Logged loss | Reference loss |
+| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| 9 | 997 | 1,958 | -0.108344980 | -0.212777812 |
+| 10 | 961 | 1,958 | 0.141537026 | 0.288376153 |
+| 21 | 926 | 1,950 | -0.183832020 | -0.387119250 |
+| 22 | 1,024 | 1,950 | 0.227126896 | 0.432517041 |
+
+All 12 steps with nonzero gradients have objective discrepancies; the maximum absolute discrepancy is **0.205390144**. The other 12 windows have zero advantages and zero gradients, so their zero losses cannot expose the normalization error. This is an optimization defect as well as a logging discrepancy: the incorrectly scaled loss is passed to backward. The installed Transformers trainer disables its own accumulation division for this trainer's non-null `compute_loss_func`, and its Accelerate accumulation factor is one, so neither supplies the missing normalization.
+
+Other observed signals:
+
+- **Execution:** `results/exit_code.txt` is 0. `results/final_metrics.json` records all 24 optimizer steps, training in 95.71 seconds, and final evaluation in 306.74 seconds, together about 402 seconds versus the 1,800-second budget. Nonzero gradient norms range from 0.7943 to 4.6454. There is no numerical or out-of-memory failure. The process-group cleanup warning occurs after completion.
+- **Held-out evidence:** final correctness is **0.1953125**, mean completion length **241.61**, and truncation fraction **0.66015625**. No initial or matched control evaluation is staged, so these numbers do not establish a performance regression caused by the normalization defect.
+- **Training and rollouts:** the 12 generation batches average correctness **0.2708333**, length **240.69**, and truncation **0.6770833**; final training-batch correctness is **0.375**. Two thirds of prompt groups have zero reward standard deviation, consistent with many zero-advantage windows. The sparse rollout examples include a correctly parsed boxed answer and two held-out answers cut off before a parseable final result. Training reward alone is insufficient evidence of held-out health.
+- **Data and rewards:** selection is the fixed seed-42 shuffled 256 training questions and first 64 test questions. All locally checked training answers and selected held-out answers parse under the supplied numerical parser. None of the 64 held-out question texts overlaps the full training split. The reward uses numerical equality after parsing. These checks did not identify a data or reward defect to repair.
+
+## Changes
+
+1. **`src/trl/trainer/grpo_trainer.py`**: added an accumulation-window preparation hook for token-normalized losses (`dapo`, `cispo`, and `vespo`). It prepares the actual microbatches before backward, sums their completion masks including any tool mask, gathers the count across processes, and assigns that shared denominator to each microbatch. Prepared dictionaries are copied so cached generation metadata is not overwritten. `_prepare_inputs` accepts these already prepared batches without regenerating or selecting another slice. Generation buffering, microbatch counter advancement, and timing accounting are preserved. The existing world-size compensation in the loss remains applicable.
+2. **`src/tests/test_grpo_accumulation.py`**: added six CPU-only regression tests with synthetic tensor rollouts. They check losses and gradients against an independently constructed window objective, unequal lengths, windows spanning generation boundaries, rollout reuse, partial windows, tool masks, all-masked windows, distributed denominator handling, evaluation behavior, and unaffected loss types. They load no language model and perform no optimizer updates.
+3. **`report.md`**: added this diagnosis, change inventory, validation, and expected effects.
+
+## Validation and expected effect
+
+All six regression tests pass. An additional in-memory CPU replay through the repaired batching and loss methods used all 24 frozen windows: maximum loss discrepancy was **5.55e-17**, maximum per-token gradient discrepancy was **0**, and 12 windows retained nonzero gradients. The replay used exactly 12 generation batches and did not modify any recorded evidence. Source syntax and shell syntax checks pass; imports resolve to `/workspace/src`. SHA-256 checks confirm `run_training.sh` and `train.py` are unchanged.
+
+The primary expected movement is **optimizer-step loss disagreement with the recomputed accumulation-window objective decreasing to numerical tolerance at every step**. For the observed nonzero windows, the corrected raw loss and gradient magnitudes increase because the denominator now excludes tokens from other updates. The signed loss can move either direction. Adam normalization and gradient clipping mean parameter-update magnitudes need not scale proportionally.
+
+The repair adds mask counting and a scalar gather without extra model forward passes or rollout generations. Completed training, nonzero updates, and final held-out evaluation should remain feasible within the existing budget. A particular held-out correctness increase or truncation decrease is not established by the staged evidence; the fresh evaluation must measure those outcomes.
+
+No training or experiment launch was performed, and no network material was fetched. Model weights, reward logic, data, configuration, launch scripts, and frozen results were not changed.
*** End Patch"));
